6. **Two independent reviews converged on the same defect class in different code paths.** This review

   `TSS_GRC_PLATFORM_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md` Phase 0 independently found it in **change
   approvals** (now **DF-4**). Neither found the other's instance. That is strong evidence the
   *class* needs a systematic sweep — every write path that accepts an actor identity — rather
   than instance-by-instance fixes. Folded into F2-22's audit scope.

## §1b Owner action register — the constraint this plan was not managing

**Round-3 review named the plan's biggest unexamined assumption: that the binding constraint is
engineering throughput.** The record says otherwise. Every *completed* item is engineer-solo work; every
*stalled* item waits on a human who is not the engineer. The plan meticulously instruments the engineering
side — ratchets, per-slice DoD, mutation proofs, a migration ledger — and had **zero instrumentation for
the other actor**. Owner-blocked items were scattered across §1, §6, §6d and §8 with no aggregate view, no
requested date and no escalation. This table is that view.

| ~~**O-5**~~ ✅ | **D-2 DECIDED — [ADR-017](TSS-GRC-Platform-Bible/Decisions/ADR-017-OWNER-DELEGATED-DECISIONS.md) D-3: 5 business days**, per-tenant overridable. Matches ITIL 4 ("next scheduled CAB") at the market-norm weekly cadence, and SAMA CSF's post-implementation review of emergency changes. Two details decided with it: the clock starts at **implementation**, not at raise; breach escalates to the CISO **and** lands in the unauthorised-change register | **S7** | earlier | Per-tenant |
| ~~**O-6**~~ ✅ | **D-9 DECIDED — [ADR-017](TSS-GRC-Platform-Bible/Decisions/ADR-017-OWNER-DELEGATED-DECISIONS.md) D-4: shelf name `Change Governance & CAB`**; `change_mgmt` stays the package name and "Change Enablement" the internal ITIL practice name. Under the ITSM name it competes with ServiceNow/Jira on CMDB and release pipelines and loses on brand | nothing (cosmetic) | 2026-07-25 | **Recommendation withdrawn** — round 2 showed "Change Enablement" is ITIL 4's own practice name. Defer to pricing time |
| **O-7** 🔶 | Commission the **independent penetration test**, **witnessed restore/failover** and **WCAG conformance statement** | 3 of the audit's own §11 acceptance gates | 2026-07-30 | **§7's "out of scope" is WITHDRAWN** ([ADR-017](TSS-GRC-Platform-Bible/Decisions/ADR-017-OWNER-DELEGATED-DECISIONS.md)): NCA ECC requires penetration testing, SAMA + NCEMA require BCM restore evidence, and a WCAG statement is table stakes for Saudi public-sector procurement — so excluding them was a silent rejection of three gates. Commissioning stays owner-only, but engineering will produce the **three specifications** (pen-test scope + RoE; restore-drill runbook + evidence template; WCAG 2.2 AA statement over the axe evidence already in `audit/`), leaving the owner to sign a vendor rather than scope a project |

**Why this table earned its place — and what happened once it existed.** The prediction was that owner
latency, not engineering throughput, set the programme's end date: Wave 2 could not start (O-3), Wave 3
could not pass S6 (O-4), and nothing new reached production at all (O-2). **Making the constraint visible
is what cleared it.** On 2026-07-30 the owner closed O-2 outright (`merge` ×5, `merge all`, then
`push all` — master is on origin), and **delegated the decision content of O-3, O-5, O-6 and the
per-finding product tail** with a standard to apply: best practice, market leaders, Saudi suitability.
[ADR-017](TSS-GRC-Platform-Bible/Decisions/ADR-017-OWNER-DELEGATED-DECISIONS.md) is that delegation
discharged — twelve decisions, each anchored to a named CMA/SAMA/NCA/PDPL control and a market-leader
precedent. **Four of the seven owner actions are now closed and two are mechanised**, leaving exactly two
things that genuinely cannot be delegated: an elevated shell (O-1) and a purchase order (O-7).

⚠ **The lesson is narrower than "delegate more".** Two items were *not* decided, on purpose: which
committee is a tenant's CAB (a charter fact — inventing it is the W2-1a-ii fabrication defect) and every
price. What was decidable in both cases was the *mechanism*: fail-closed configuration for the first,
paid-vs-Base for the second. **The blocker was rarely the fact; it was the absence of a rule for the fact's
absence** — and that rule was always the engineer's to write. The programme's
end date becomes independent of engineering pace, and §1's "where we actually are" keeps meaning *where the
branch is*, which is not where the product is. Finding 1 (the staged jar) is that gap's first casualty.

**Make owner latency as visible as the authorisation ratchet.** Update `Requested` and add a waiting-days
column at each review.

## §2 The decision that gated a third of this plan — ANSWERED

**D-3 · Is the commercial model per-module SKUs, or a single suite licence?**
→ **Per-module SKUs, one deployment, one database.** [ADR-013](TSS-GRC-Platform-Bible/Decisions/ADR-013-PER-MODULE-SKU-AND-ENTITLEMENT.md), 2026-07-25.

So the left column below is now the live plan: **F2-04, F2-05 and F2-06 are Wave 2 as written**, ADR-009…012
are adopted, and the 11 Saudi Tier-B modules are the first SKUs. **D-3 no longer gates Wave 2, and neither does F2-35 any more** — ✅ **ratified 2026-07-30 by [ADR-018](TSS-GRC-Platform-Bible/Decisions/ADR-018-SKU-CATALOGUE-RATIFICATION.md)**. The three contradictory catalogues are superseded by [`Product/SKU_CATALOGUE.md`](TSS-GRC-Platform-Bible/Product/SKU_CATALOGUE.md). **Wave 2 has no remaining decision blocker** — W2-0 is writable (see its row for the one measured backfill it must carry).

| Consequence | Detail |
|---|---|
| Wave 2 is unblocked *by D-3* | F2-04 / F2-05 / F2-06 proceed at P1. ✅ **F2-35's catalogue ratified 2026-07-30 (ADR-018)** — the last decision gate is gone |
| One item is **added ahead of F2-04** | **W2-0 grandfather licence backfill.** Orgs 2 and 3 hold exactly one licence row each (`SOCOPS`); `@RequireModule` is fail-closed, so annotating controllers before backfilling would black out two of three tenants |
| The SKU catalogue moves out of code | `LicensingService.KNOWN_MODULES` is a hard-coded `Set.of` of 20 codes that calls itself the source of truth — a recompile per SKU. It moves into the module registry (F2-01) |
| Two other decisions dissolved | **D-4** (`incident` joins the Cyber & SOC *SKU*; the package does not move, so F2-06b is no longer gated) and **D-6** (no role bypasses entitlement — platform administration is inside the mandatory Base SKU, so there is nothing to bypass) |

Pricing is **not** decided and is not this plan's business. *(Assessment Part 3 §9 lists the other business
questions.)*

### §1c Root causes — why the queue is now ordered by cause, not by finding

**Seventeen `F2-*` items were opened or closed on 2026-07-31. They are not seventeen problems.**
⚠ **This line said *twenty-one* and the review could not reproduce it — correctly.** Counting from the table's own columns: **15 opened** (F2-58…F2-72) **+ 2 closed that were opened earlier** (F2-55 refuted, F2-56 fixed) = **17**. Twenty-one needed three non-`F2` items (A17-D5, A17-D10b, O-1) silently folded in. A round number in the first sentence of a root-cause analysis is exactly where a reader stops checking, which is why it is worth correcting rather than quietly dropping.
Mapped to cause, they are four — plus four habits of method that produced the *analysis* errors,
including several of mine. Ordering the queue by finding meant paying for the same cause repeatedly;
this table is why the ordering principle changed.

| # | Root cause | Findings it produced | Enforced now by | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **RC-A** | **Two schema authorities that never reconcile.** Dev is Python-bootstrapped with Flyway **off**; prod runs Flyway **on**, baselined at 292 over a restored dev dump. So **any migration numbered ≤ 292 can never execute in either environment**, and anything the Python bootstrap creates exists nowhere else | **F2-49** (2 migrations Flyway never applies) · **F2-64** (crisis-comms: 3 pages over absent tables) · **F2-65** (V247's drop can never run) · **F2-70** (**67 mapped tables no migration creates**) · **F2-71** (4 more, incl. Nafath SSO, with live controllers) · **F2-72** (column drift) — **six** | `schema_drift.py` (intent vs schema) + `SchemaContractRatchetTest` (DB-free, in CI) | 🔶 **THE CONSEQUENCE IS CLOSED; THE CAUSE IS NOT — corrected 2026-08-07, and the distinction is why this is a root-cause row rather than a finding.** ✔ `flyway:migrate` **does** build this platform now: **360 files run V1 → V373 on an empty database**, and F2-70, F2-75, F2-77, F2-143, F2-153 and F2-154 are all closed. The two authorities reconcile on every measured axis (F2-153's closing measurement: CHECK dev 417 / built 414, FK 185 / 178, UNIQUE-by-property 271 / 268, **extra 0** — every remaining difference a deliberate exclusion). So the sentence this cell carried for weeks, *"no customer can be deployed who was not cloned from this laptop"*, is **no longer true**. ⚠ **What is still true is the cause**: dev remains Python-bootstrapped with Flyway off and prod remains baselined, so the two schemas are still maintained by different mechanisms and can still diverge — which is precisely what `schema_convergence.py` now measures, and what caught F2-146 and F2-153. ⚠ And the *deployed* gap is a separate item: prod is **29 migrations behind (V345–V373)**, which is **O-1**, not RC-A. 🔑 A root cause whose worst consequence has been fixed must not be recorded as closed — the mechanism that produced six findings is still in place, and the instrument is what changed |

Batching them behind one restart is a defensible call — **marking F2-71 ✅ DONE while it is dev-only is not, because it breaks the very DoD this row states.** A cause with a detector is *permanent*; it can be instrumented and it cannot be finished. ➕ **And on 2026-08-01 the detector itself turned out to be blind — `F2-73`:** `/actuator/info` could not read `platform.flyway_schema_history` (unqualified table name → empty `dbo`), so `pending` was structurally always empty and `deployment_identity.py`'s "packaged but NOT applied" check **could never fire in the only environment RC-B is about**. Fixed same day. **A cause is not instrumented because an instrument exists; it is instrumented when the instrument has been shown to fire.** |

The 🔑 line below named this pattern and then declined to make it a row, which is how a cause stays invisible while being described |

#### The method causes — these produced the analysis errors, several of them mine

| Habit | Where it bit today | The discipline that replaces it |
|---|---|---|
| **Regex without context** | my `V93` false positive (a `DROP` that re-creates); 418 vs 417 vs 413 entity counts from three greps; **`MAPPED_NO_TABLE = 0` when it was 4**, because the parser demanded `schema=` and stopped at the first `)` | reflection over compiled annotations; strip comments; match parentheses; **anti-vacuity floors, with anchors that cannot expire** |
| **Measuring a component and reporting the system** | `iterator().next()` on a `HashSet` (F2-54); my own `board-pack.json` audit claim; **re-issuing V12–V14 verbatim** — the DDL was *a* truth, not the *current* one | probe the whole path live; derive claims from evidence the tool already holds, never assert them in a string |
| **A mock that builds an impossible world** | my clone test passed against an empty visible list that cannot occur — live probe said 409, test said 400 | if a mocked state is unreachable, the test proves nothing |
| **Prose as the source of truth** | §1/§8 wrong twice about the staged jar; `MEASURED_BASELINE.md` stale by 21 migrations and wrong about the baseline (V312 vs **292**) | generate registers; validate allowlists **both** ways; make the running process answer |

🔑 **The pattern under all eight: the control existed and the enforcement did not.** Every one of
these was preventable by something already in the repo. The proof is that `vitest` was **absent from
CI** — six frontend test files, including the route-reachability guard that found 8 unreachable
screens, had never run there. **A ratchet nobody runs is a comment.** Fixed 2026-07-31; the standing
rule is that a new control ships with the thing that fails when it is violated.

### Wave 0b — the ADR-017 implementation queue *(ordered 2026-07-30; order **debated**, not asserted)*

ADR-017 settled twelve owner-blocked decisions. D-1/D-4/D-6/D-7/D-9/D-11/D-12 are closed or deferred with a
stated condition. **These five remained unsequenced**, so they were measured, then put to a three-seat
Fable 5 council (Saudi-regulatory / exploitability / commercial lenses) with my proposed order as the target
to attack. **Both surviving seats changed the order, and measurement then overturned two of the council's own
claims.** The provenance of every change is recorded here because the order is now load-bearing.

⚠ **The delivery boundary is the restart, not the commit.** Seat A's strongest point: I was sequencing
commits while an examiner sequences *production states*. Prod runs the 2026-07-23 jar; everything below
lands in one batch whenever O-1 happens. So "first" means *first into the batch*, and an item that is ready
must not miss the batch while a larger item is in flight.

| # | ID | Action | Size | Status | Migration |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

**What the council got wrong, and how.** Both errors were caught by measuring its claims instead of adopting them —
the same discipline that killed D-11.

- **"The board pack contains named AML alerts and ethics-case detail, which do not belong in a board pack at
  any tier."** **False, and my brief caused it** — I listed "ethics cases, AML alerts" among the contents and
  the seat reasonably read that as itemised. Measured: ethics and AML enter only as `count*` calls
  (`countByOrganisationIdAndCategory` for bribery/kickback/retaliation, `countByOrganisationIdAndStrFiled`).
  It is aggregate MI, exactly as the seat said a board pack should be. **The composition point survives in a
  better-evidenced form** → **F2-55**: the pack carries up to **200 itemised risks** and up to **1,000
  itemised audit findings**, which is an operational extract, not board MI.
- **"Board-pack downloads are unminuted."** **False.** `ExportAuditInterceptor` is registered on `/api/**`
  and writes `action_type='EXPORT'` to `platform.audit_log`; **366 EXPORT events exist, 72 of them
  board-pack**. The control exists and is queryable — which is what made the look-back runnable at all.
  ➕ But running it found a real defect the council could not have predicted → **F2-54**.

D-8's direction (it widens), the exception-tier populations (`PRIVACY` 8/59, `IAM` 3/59, so the baseline is
the problem and not the exceptions), and the machine-account comparison (`WORKFLOW:EXPORT` 55/59 including
8 machine accounts is the wider grant, but the board pack is the more sensitive payload — both are in D-10a).

ledger across four documents will keep drifting. The mechanical check below is the only reliable authority.

**Reservations are advisory; ordering is not.** A number is only real when the file exists. Treat every row
above as *intent*, and immediately before creating a file run:

```bash
ls tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/sqlserver | sed 's/^V\([0-9]*\)__.*/\1/' | sort -n | tail -1
```

**Never author a number below an already-applied migration** — Flyway applies in version order and would
skip it. Corollary the council had to point out: **if item A is delivered before item B, A takes the lower
number**, no matter which has the earlier ID.

**Rules.** Additive only unless explicitly authorised. Idempotent. Applied to dev **twice** via pyodbc
(Flyway is off in dev). It is verbatim the defect F2-69 files against `MEASURED_BASELINE.md`, living inside the plan that files it.** The baseline is load-bearing: it decides which migrations can *never* run, which is the whole of RC-A. Read it from `platform.flyway_schema_history`, never from prose. `flyway.clean` is disabled; never run it. Every destructive change needs
a reverse recipe in the file header and the user's explicit OK.

⚠ **Reserved numbers move.** `V316` was reserved for `ck_change_status`, then taken by DF-4; `V317` was

plan section, before writing a migration — and re-check it immediately before the file is created.

## §5 Definition of done — per slice, not per stage

A slice is done when **all** of these hold. This is the standard every completed programme in §0 met.

1. **Full backend suite green** before and after (`mvn -o clean package`, ~2,250+ tests; grep the log for
   `BUILD SUCCESS` / `Tests run:` — wrapper exit codes lie).
2. **Live-probed against the running stack** — Python `urllib` + `pyodbc`, through the Vite proxy (`:5173`)
   when verifying browser behaviour. Guard **403**s and SoD **409**s are part of the probe, not exceptions
   to it; four-eyes paths need **two users** (`admin` + `so_officer`).
3. **The net is proven real** — temporarily break the new guard/check and confirm a test fails, then
   restore. A test that cannot fail is not evidence.
4. **Migrations applied to dev twice** and idempotent.
5. **Ratchets not worsened** — authorisation coverage ≤ 21, plus (once added) tightness, boundary edges,
   mock imports, page size, i18n, accessibility.
6. **Bilingual** `*_en` + `*_ar` on any new user-visible record, client-gated in the form.
7. **Committed per slice** on a feature branch, with the probe result in the message.

## §6 Open decisions

**Six of eight are now decided** (2026-07-25), on the owner's instruction to adopt the leader-aligned
best-practice default rather than keep a third of the plan blocked. Each carries an ADR with the
comparator evidence, the alternatives, the trade-offs accepted and its reversal cost.

### Decided

| # | Decision | Answer | ADR |
|---|---|---|---|
| **D-3** | Per-module SKUs or suite-only? | **Per-module SKUs, one deployment, one database**, enforced by the `@RequireModule` aspect that already exists; a **mandatory Base Platform SKU**; the catalogue moves from `LicensingService.KNOWN_MODULES` (`Set.of`, needs a recompile) into the module registry; **grandfather backfill first** — orgs 2/3 hold one licence row each, so annotating before backfilling is an outage. Pricing explicitly out of scope | [ADR-013](TSS-GRC-Platform-Bible/Decisions/ADR-013-PER-MODULE-SKU-AND-ENTITLEMENT.md) |
| **D-4** | `incident` — separate SKU or part of Cyber? | **Dissolved.** A SKU is a commercial view over packages, so this was never architectural. `incident` joins the **Cyber & SOC** SKU; the package does not move. **F2-06b is no longer gated on this** and is judged purely on ADR-011 | ADR-013 |
| **D-6** | Does `PLATFORM_ADMIN` bypass entitlement? | **No — never, for any role.** The question dissolves: platform administration lives in the mandatory Base SKU, so there is nothing to bypass. One rule beats a role-dependent one, and it is what Salesforce does | ADR-013 |
| **D-7** | Which roles may cast a committee vote? | **Roster confers the vote; the grant opens the door.** `ADMIN:APPROVE` created (**15 roles**); `ADMIN:WRITE` cut to the **secretariat (3)** because it also appoints member terms — the same grant did both, so any voter could add themselves to a roster and manufacture a quorum. `ADMIN:READ` **21**, `ADMIN:EXPORT` **7**. `INTERNAL_AUDITOR` gets READ+EXPORT but **no vote** (IIA 1110 independence) | [ADR-014](TSS-GRC-Platform-Bible/Decisions/ADR-014-COMMITTEE-VOTING-RIGHTS.md) |
| **D-8** | Which roles may cast a CAB vote? | **Guard stays `CHANGE:APPROVE`; the grant was the defect.** Created the missing ITIL **`CHANGE_MANAGER`** role and took `CHANGE:APPROVE` from **3 → 9**: +CHANGE_MANAGER, SERVICE_OWNER, CISO, CYBER_MANAGER, COMPLIANCE_OFFICER, EXECUTIVE_REVIEWER. Safe to widen because DF-4's provenance controls carry the load | [ADR-015](TSS-GRC-Platform-Bible/Decisions/ADR-015-CHANGE-AUTHORITY-AND-CAB-VOTING.md) |
| **Doc governance** | How is the 335-document corpus governed? *(was "provisional")* | **Docs-as-code, one canonical doc per subject, machine-checked.** Status header on every `.md` (`AUTHORITATIVE`/`GENERATED`/`HISTORIC`/`SUPERSEDED-BY`), supersede-never-delete, generated files never hand-edited, every quantitative claim cites its command, register CI-enforced. Grounded in ISO 27001 §7.5 — *the clause this product sells* | [ADR-016](TSS-GRC-Platform-Bible/Decisions/ADR-016-DOCUMENTATION-GOVERNANCE.md) |

**D-5** (which Saudi integration pack generation governs — root 20 files vs `docs/` 33) is **downgraded
from a decision to a task** under W0-6: ADR-016 R2/R3 supply the rule, so it needs a content diff and a
`SUPERSEDED-BY` header, not a judgement call.

Merge and push have been separate authorisations all along and that is deliberate; the risk is that the gap now compounds silently, and **no `W-*` or `F2-*` id owns it** (the second-model review found this by counting commits, not by reading any row). Either a one-off "push" or a standing rule; the plan cannot assume either | Deployment durability | Product owner |

A real invitation means token + mail + accept + set-password, **plus** a decision on who may invite: `POST /api/v1/admin/users` is `hasRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN')` today, so the tenant admin running onboarding cannot create users at all. The alternative — generating other people's initial passwords and displaying them — is a credentials decision and is not a UI fix. The false promise is already removed either way | F2-33's capability half | Product owner |

D-1 and D-2 are per-customer charter facts. Inventing them would be fabricating governance data, which
is the defect F2-02 exists to record. D-4 is a product decision about a capability, and the same rule
applies: the screen now describes what it does rather than what it would do if the subsystem existed.

**This closes the reconciliation the Bible's `README` marked "provisional and unconfirmed".** Every finding
in [`TSS_GRC_PLATFORM_AUDIT_REPORT.md`](TSS-GRC-Platform-Bible/TSS_GRC_PLATFORM_AUDIT_REPORT.md) §10 was
re-derived from source and from the running system on 2026-07-25, using that document's own truth labels.
Nothing was accepted because it was written down, including the parts that flatter this plan.

So a `CHANGE:WRITE` holder can *advance* a legitimately-decided change but cannot *manufacture* the decision. The literal claim — a generic transition guarded by `WRITE` reaching privileged states — is still true. **Critical → P1, downgrading to P2 only when F2-28 closes.** The council overturned an unconditional P2: `CAB_APPROVED` has two legitimating legs — recorded votes (sound after DF-4) *or* a quorate committee resolution — and the second leg rests on `quorumMet`, which F2-28 proves is caller-authored. **Verdict on the strategic frame: sound, and worth having.** Its structural measurements reproduce almost
exactly. Three findings needed correction (F-002, F-009, F-011), one was materially understated (F-008),
one is unverified (F-010) — and **one caught a live P0 that this register's own first pass missed** (F-003's
quorum half). That is the second time the two passes have caught different instances of the *same* defect
class in different code, which retires any argument that one of them is redundant.

### Rating, re-judged

The audit's 3.0/5 was fair at its baseline. On measured change since:

| Dimension | Audit | Now | Why |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Security / control integrity | 1.8 | **2.3** | 2 of its 7 critical weaknesses closed with mutation proof and live probes, 1 mitigated — but a live P0 forgery chain on the governance backbone (F2-28), a platform-wide least-privilege inversion (F2-27) and 214 unaudited mass-assignment sites do not support 2.6. Council: "2.2–2.4 is the defensible band"; I had written "movement is real but narrow" and then awarded +0.8 |
| Commercial packaging | 2.4 | **2.6** | still 22 of 252 controllers, but the decision is made (ADR-013) and the mechanism is proven fail-closed |
| Quality / operations | 3.2 | **3.4** | +144 tests, adversarial governance tests, mutation-proven guards; operational evidence still absent |
| Enterprise architecture | 2.6 | **2.6** | unchanged — pairs and cycles improved marginally, no architecture test yet |
| **Weighted** | **3.0** | **≈3.05** | Movement is real but narrow. **Still `Qualified`** |

**Market verdict, changed in one place:** the audit made a controlled pilot conditional on Criticals
closing. F-001 is closed and F-002 is mitigated — but **F2-28 is a new open Critical**, so *"pilot after
Criticals close"* still holds and now has a specific, costed blocker: 3–5 days, sequenced behind F2-25 (2 h)
and F2-26 (1 d). General availability, government final acceptance and per-module sale verdicts are
**unchanged**.

History is **labelled, never rewritten**: 3,317 rows → `LEGACY_UNRECORDED`, 2,748 → `LEGACY_AUTHORITY_SAMPLE`. | **F2-58** | found sizing D-5, 2026-07-31 | **The board pack is computed twice by two renderers that can disagree, and both rank a paged sample rather than the register.** Measured: `reporting.BoardPackService` (554 lines, **35** repository call sites, 11 repositories + `SustainabilityDashboardService`) and `reporting.BoardPackPptxService` (406 lines, **32** call sites, **8 of the same repositories**) each build the whole aggregate independently. There is no shared aggregate object — `BoardPackService` exposes only `generatePdf(String)` returning `byte[]`, and every `render*` method queries and renders in one pass. So the PDF and the PPTX deck **of the same board pack** are two implementations of one document and are free to drift; they already differ on population (PDF top **20** risks, PPTX top **10**) and on method (PPTX derives `openFindings` by fetching 1,000 rows and filtering in Java; the PDF builds aging counters from its own 1,000-row fetch; neither uses a `count` query, and the PPTX issues a 1,000-row page purely to read `getTotalElements()`). ➕ **The sharper defect: `findByOrganisationId(org, PageRequest.of(0, 200))` carries no `Sort`.** The 200 rows are whatever order SQL Server returns; the code then sorts *that page* by inherent score and takes the top 20. So **"Risk Register — Top 20" is the top 20 of an arbitrary 200-row sample**, not of the register — and a board receiving it has no way to tell. Same shape for findings at 1,000. ⚠ **Latent, not live, and the distinction is the point:** measured on **both** databases, the largest tenant holds **51 risks** (cap 200) and **41 findings** (cap 1,000) — dev and prod identical. Nothing is wrong in any board pack today. It goes wrong silently at risk 201, with no error and no log line, which is the worst way for a board report to fail. **This is D-5's central design constraint, which is why it was found before D-5 was built:** exposing the aggregate as JSON means choosing one of the two implementations, so the DTO extraction must **collapse both renderers onto one `buildAggregate()`** — and it is worthless if it enshrines the paged-sample ranking. Fix: rank in the database, or count with `count` queries; then have PDF, PPTX and JSON render one aggregate | M | ✅ **DONE 2026-07-31 — correctness half @`859efb2f`, duplication half @`b99a3d53` (D-5).** Ranking now happens in SQL in **both** renderers: `PageRequest.of(0, 20 or 10, Sort.by(DESC,"inherentScore").and(ASC,"id"))`. The id tiebreaker is new and deliberate — several risks share a score and the old in-memory sort broke ties by the arbitrary page order, so the pack could name a different 20th risk on two runs over unchanged data. Aging tiers now come from a new `countOpenByOrganisationIdOlderThan` over **every** open finding, and the 15-row table from `findOldestOpenByOrganisationId`, which excludes CLOSED in SQL — the old page counted only open rows toward its 15 but paged over both, so a tenant whose first 1,000 findings were mostly closed could render fewer than 15 while older open ones sat unlisted. PPTX `totalRisks` / `openFindings` / `closed` moved to `count` queries (one had been issuing a 1,000-row page purely to read `getTotalElements()`). ➕ **Proven live at the volume that matters, not asserted:** 210 `[REVIEW-TEST]` risks seeded to put org 1 at **261**, arranged so that **0 of the 9 highest-scoring risks fell inside the unordered 200-row window** — i.e. the old code would have rendered a board "Top 20" containing **none** of the worst risks. The generated PDF and PPTX were then parsed (pypdf / slide XML): all five apex risks present in both, no score-1 filler, aging **2/8/0/28**. Seed removed with `CHARINDEX`; org counts back to 51/10/10. ⚠ **Two of my own reference values were wrong and the code was right — both worth keeping.** (i) The aging reference omitted **`is_deleted = 0`**, which the entity's `@Where` enforces and which exactly one finding in the 30–59 tier is subject to — landmine 6 in CLAUDE.md, and it surfaced only because I trusted the code over my expectation instead of "fixing" the code to match. (ii) Three hand-computed cutoff dates were each a day out; the property test arbitrated. `cutoff()` is **shared, not duplicated** — same package, so the PPTX calls `BoardPackService.cutoff`. `BoardPackAgingCutoffTest` (3 tests) pins the day-vs-timestamp boundary across 4×131×3 cases, because `now().minusDays(N)` is the natural translation and is off by one for any finding created later in the day than the report runs. ✅ **The duplication half shipped too, in D-5 @`b99a3d53` (2026-07-31)** — both renderers now render one `BoardPackAggregateService.build(Scope)`, so the 35 and 32 independent call sites are gone and the PDF, the deck and the new JSON aggregate cannot disagree. **F2-58 is fully closed.** |

notices changes to itself; it cannot prove its definition matches the world.** Nor did “two
implementations agree” help — both shared the same *definition*, so agreement was worthless. Now: a

and **(a)'s blast radius in dev is zero** — the three ACCEPTED risks are LOW/LOW/MEDIUM and within
appetite, so the gate never applied to them, against the finding's *"will refuse closes that succeed
today… needs the owner's word"*. Also measured: **all four APPROVED acceptance rows in the database
belong to soft-deleted probe risks**, so no acceptance has ever been recorded through the UI — which is
what an unreachable approval step looks like from the data side.

✔ **2026-08-09 — [[F2-172]] CLOSED (P2): the intake front door became real — and it was broken at
both ends at once, which is why it took two slices and a merge.** F2-171's follow-up said the fix was
to "call `POST /api/v1/intake` on submit and `PUT …/triage` on triage". **Measuring what that rewire
would actually hit, before writing it, is what turned a chore into the finding.** Three defects would
have shipped as regressions from a mechanical repointing:

**(a)** the server accepted **16** of the frontend's **26** intake kinds — the ten it rejected are the
DD-88 HRSD and DD-94 MOC workflows, including the **24-hour GOSI workplace-injury notification** and
the **WPS payroll confirmation**, both statutory — while `IntakeService`'s javadoc claimed the two
catalogues were mirrored (they were, once, at DD-82). ⚙ *Two copies of a routing table where only one
side is exercised do not drift slowly; they drift completely and silently.* `IntakeKindRouting` is
pinned to `intake.ts` field-by-field in both directions now.

**(b)** `POST /api/v1/intake` was guarded by `INTAKE:WRITE`, **held by 3 of 69 roles, all
administrators**, so repointing the client would have 403'd every employee reporting a security event
(NCA ECC 6.1) or a privacy breach (PDPL Art. 27). Opened to `isAuthenticated()` under **ADR-010
§Sanctioned exceptions** — it *subsumes* `CoiController#submitDeclaration`, admitted for the same
reason at F2-144(b), so the argument did not have to be constructed, only noticed — with V374's
`submitter_user_id` landing **first**, for F2-144's reason. The sharper half has no COI counterpart:
`submitterIsAnonymous` also arrived from the body, and obeying it unconditionally would let any caller
make any submission unattributable through the field that exists to protect whistleblowers, so it is
honoured only where the catalogue allows it and nothing identifying is stored when it is.

**(c)** *"Promotion creates the target row"* was implemented on **neither side**. `IntakeService.triage()`
read `promotedToEntityType`/`promotedToRecordId` **out of the request body** and created nothing, under
a DTO comment saying they were *"echoed back so the frontend can deeplink to the new register row"* — a
sentence that assumes a row. 🔑 **The fix is a boundary decision, not a rewire.** Seam =
`intake.spi.RegisterPromotionPort` declared in **Base**, implemented by **13 adapters living in the
module that OWNS the record** (`privacy/intake/`, `risk/intake/`…). ADR-018 homes `intake` in Base and
12 of the 14 targets are sold SKUs, so importing them from intake would make the mandatory kernel
depend on commercial modules. The `CHANGE` adapter sits in `change_adapters` because
**`ChangeModuleBoundaryTest` refused the obvious placement** — an existing guard catching a real design
question. Four properties bought: target from the **kind's catalogue entry**; id from **the row that
was written**; the **target module's own write permission** on top of `INTAKE:TRIAGE`; and a target
with no adapter is a **409 naming it**. ⚠ Guessing the permission from the target name is the trap —
the ethics register and the whole `policy` module are guarded by **`COMPLIANCE:WRITE`**, and `ETHICS`
*does* exist in the catalogue, so the obvious guess compiles and 403s.

⚙ **The slice boundary was set by a test, not by me.** The server half was scoped server-only, planning
the client rewire as a follow-up; `FrontendEndpointContractTest` refused the commit because `GET /{id}`
had no caller — a ceiling firing in the direction a ceiling normally cannot, and a better scoping
decision than my own.

✔ **2026-08-09 — [[F2-171]] CLOSED (P2): pressing "Promote" on an intake writes the register
row to `localStorage` and to nothing else — with a POSITIVE id, on eleven registers that render
live governance buttons.** Opened out of [[F2-170]]'s residue, which listed `dpiaApi.create` among
16 entities "no screen can create". That framing was wrong in a way only reading the page could
show: `PrivacyPage.tsx:323` says *"DD-76: route DSR / breach / DPIA creation through Services
Center"* — creation is **deliberately** routed to intake, and the client method is dark **because
that other path exists.** Following it is the whole finding. The other path does not reach the
server: `triage(…, 'PROMOTE', …)` calls `addPromoted()`, which writes browser storage, and the
intake record's permanent history note then reads *"Promoted to DPIA #482913"* — an id belonging
to no record. Live-probed: `GET /api/v1/intake` answers **200 with totalElements 0**, and
`intake.intake_records` holds **0 rows**, because `IntakeController` + `IntakeService` were built
(DD-82), are reachable, and **no product code has ever called them**. The service's own javadoc
says it implements the lifecycle "the React `useIntake()` hook drives"; nothing drives it.

🔑 **Three files gave three accounts of one value, and the live one was the unsafe one.**
`promotedAdapters.ts` opened by promising *negative* ids "so they never collide with
backend-assigned ids"; `PromotedRecord.id` promised "highest existing + 1"; `intake.ts` minted
`Date.now() % 1_000_000`, positive, in exactly the range IDENTITY values occupy — and all twelve
numeric adapters passed it straight through. **The file documenting the hazard was the file
letting it through**, [[F2-168]]'s shape exactly. Precisely one of thirteen adapters honoured the
contract. Harms in order of certainty: nothing persists (every promotion); the row's Approve /
Submit / Reject / Expire buttons address a nonexistent id, so the governance chain cannot proceed
(every promotion); the title linked to `/dpias/<synthetic>`; and — measured at **0.056% of
promotions in dev, growing linearly with tenant size** — the id names a *real, unrelated* record
and approves it while the screen shows the promoted row's title.

⚠ **Five fabrication guards were green, each having measured a different property of the same
defect class.** [[F2-137]] scopes to `/portal/` and `/public/` routes; this path is authenticated
throughout, so its premise test ("`lib/intake` really does make zero network calls") had measured
the fact while its scope excluded the consequence. [[F2-167]] disables actions on fabricated rows
but resolves on the **demo** flag, and a promoted row is not demo. `demoFallbackContract` matches
`/mock/i` in the import path, and this store is named after the domain it fakes.
[[F2-168]]/[[F2-169]] swept the mock corpus, which this is not in. **A fourth source of fabricated
rows that no fabrication guard measured.** The reusable question is not "is there a guard?" but
"which existing guard's *scope* excludes this?"

Fixed in two layers, and only one is the control: `assertNotPlaceholder()` at **all three**
network entry points in `lib/api.ts` refuses a negative-id path before `fetch` and throws an
error that names the cause — total, so whatever a page misses cannot leave the browser; plus
`mintPromotedId()` negative by construction, `promotedId()` coercing on read (localStorage has no
migration step, so pre-fix overlays are repaired rather than trusted), and 15 row-action sites +
the DPIA tab made inert and labelled. Browser-verified with a seeded promotion: both PDPL buttons
`disabled`, no link, an Arabic "غير محفوظ" badge — while all **six real DPIAs on the same screen**
kept their links and live buttons, which is the negative control that makes the first half mean
anything. ⚠ Two of my own assertions shipped **vacuous** and only mutation found them (a
query-string case that passed whether or not the query was stripped — twice, with two different
values), and **my mutation harness misreported 11 of 12 results** because vitest's `Tests N
failed` line is ANSI-coloured. Follow-up **F2-172** filed to make promotion persist; note the
server's `triage()` takes `promotedToRecordId` from the client and creates nothing, so the target
row is created on **neither** side.

✔ **F2-177 CLOSED 2026-08-09 — the last three ghost role names were committee seats, and three of
the four things needed to ask that question had already shipped for other reasons.** [[F2-52]] drained
the ghost-role population from 40 to 3 over six slices and stopped, because the survivors
(`AUDIT_COMMITTEE_CHAIR`, `AUDIT_COMMITTEE_MEMBER`, `AUDIT_DIRECTOR`) resist all three of its routes:
seating them as roles admits every holder to every committee's business, dropping the legs discards the
only record of who the endpoint is for, and converting to a module permission hands the access to
every reader of the module. [[F2-159]]'s entity ownership does not fit either — the guarded record is
not the committee, it is a pivot or an overview the committee *reviews*, so there is no owner column.

The fourth route is `hasPermission('AUDIT_COMMITTEE','COMMITTEE','SEAT')`: a **second relation** on the
four-argument overload, dispatched on `targetType`, answered from `admin.committee_member_terms`. Six
sites, both controllers in `module.governance`, all reads — and `RiskControlFindingPivotController`'s
own javadoc had said for months that the view exists for *"audit-committee preparation"*, which was
true of the intent and false of the guard.

🔑 **The register recorded "no SpEL function asks the question yet" and that sentence became the size
of the job.** Measured: [[F2-26]] had linked roster seats to platform users, [[F2-28]] had made the
roster the quorum denominator, and S6c had already normalised the free-text seat title (16 distinct
spellings over 43 seats, three meaning *chair*). None was authorisation work; together they were
everything this needed, and the remaining cost was one interface, one component and two queries —
about what [[F2-161]]'s second ownership resolver cost, for the same reason. **Re-measure a recorded
blocker before believing its estimate.**

⚠ **And the number that matters is the one the guard cannot fix.** Of 43 seats in dev, **13** name a
platform user, 1 is declared external and **29 do neither**; `AUDIT_COMMITTEE` is **0 of 5**, and
production is **0 of 31 — no committee seat is linked to any platform user at all.** So the leg answers
`false` for every caller today, exactly as unreachable as the ghost it replaced. What changed is that a
tenant administrator can now fix it from the roster screen instead of needing a jar. Filed as
**F2-178** rather than left as a caveat, because a fix whose value depends on data nobody has entered
needs saying out loud.

⚠ **The remedy could have rebuilt the defect inside itself**: `'AUDIT_COMMITTE'` — one letter short —
is a permanently false leg in exactly the way a ghost role name is. `CommitteeSeatGuardTest` pins the
17-value `committee_type` vocabulary at a hard zero and pins `SEAT` as the only relation, because
**replacing an unvalidated string with a different unvalidated string is not a fix.** `AUDIT_DIRECTOR`
also had to have its *intent* recovered rather than its name fixed: it is the head of internal audit,
whom this platform models as `INTERNAL_AUDITOR` — already named in the same guard — so deleting it
removed a duplicate, not an authority.

Ghost role names in `@PreAuthorize` **3 → 0** (now an invariant, not a ratchet) and on the attachment

🔶 **F2-178 — the visibility half CLOSED 2026-08-09, and the slice's own register row is the lesson.**
F2-177 filed F2-178 three hours earlier recommending "a linkage-coverage report on the committee
screen — per committee, seats linked / declared external / neither". **That report shipped with
[[F2-26]]**: `GET /committees/registry/committees/{id}/linkage` has returned exactly those three

*re-measure a recorded blocker before believing its estimate* — was repeated by F2-177's own
recommendation, on the same day, by the session that wrote the lesson.** Writing a lesson down does
not transfer it; **a recommendation is the least-verified claim on the register**, because nothing
executes it.

⚙ What was genuinely missing was narrower and sharper: the report could only be read **one committee at
a time**. Production is **0 of 31 seats linked** and finding that out meant opening seventeen registry
screens in turn, so nobody did. `GET /api/v1/committees/registry/linkage-coverage` + `RosterCoveragePanel`
now answer it in one call, worst-first. And a **state a per-committee report structurally cannot show**:
`linkage(committeeId)` takes an id, so "empty roster" and "0% linked" arrive as the same screen —
**9 of 18** live dev committees and **11 of 17** production committees have *no term rows at all*, which
means they can never be quorate and is what `ChangeGovernanceHealthService.ROSTER_EMPTY` already refuses
CAB approvals for.

⚠⚠ **Measuring it found a second defect with a date on it.** F2-26's report counts a seat by
`renewal_status = 'ACTIVE'`; F2-177's guard *also* requires `ended_at IS NULL` and today inside the term
window — **two consumers of one column deciding "this seat counts" by different rules**, so a roster can
read **100% covered and admit nobody**. The rule this breaks was already in the tree, written for a
different pair: `ChangeGovernanceHealthService` says *"a report describing access must share its
predicate with the enforcement point"*, after [[F2-62]] cost exactly that. The divergence is **0 rows
today** — and **nothing in this platform ever moves an ACTIVE term to EXPIRED** (the sweep only sends
reminders; `endTerm` is manual), so it arrives by calendar arithmetic: **the earliest production term
ends 2027-03-01.** Both queries are now built by concatenation from one `CURRENT_SEAT_WINDOW` constant,
and `SeatWindowPredicateSharingTest` fails the build if the clause appears **twice** in the repository
source — a copy reads as correct on the day it is written, which is why it needs a build failure rather
than a review comment.

➕ Two smaller ones. Java strips **trailing** whitespace inside text blocks, so the first draft emitted
`WHENt.endedAt` and a malformed `@Query` **fails at context startup** — the whole application, not one
endpoint; both constants now lead with their own newline so no caller can lose the separator. And the
probe's org-2 fixture tagged `[REVIEW-TEST]` in `name_en` while its `DELETE` matched on `code`, orphaning
a committee and two seats in another tenant **while the tag-check leg passed** — caught only by printing
the before/after count. 🔑 *The `CHARINDEX` convention holds only if the tag is in the column the cleanup
matches on*; the leak is now a failing leg. 13 + 9 + 10 new tests, live probe **30/30** including the
divergence forced on real rows and cross-tenant isolation against a second-tenant committee created for
it. No migration. ⚠ **Still open and not an engineering act:** somebody has to do the linking.

⚠⚠ **Correction 2026-08-10 — two of that slice's own tests were wrong for three hours of every day.**
`CommitteeSeatLinkageTest` built its seat-currency fixtures with `LocalDate.now()`, which resolves in the
JVM's default zone (Riyadh, **UTC+3**), while the service reads `LocalDate.now(clock)` on
`Clock.system(ZoneId.of("UTC"))`. Between local midnight and 03:00 they differ by a day, so a term ending
"yesterday" was still current and `currentSeats()` came back **2 where 1 was asserted**. It merged **green**
and failed a day later, during F2-175's suite run at 00:4x local — inside the only window that could
reveal it. 🔑 **Same lesson as F2-178's own, from the other side:** that slice recorded *a fixed-clock test
whose fixed date equals the real date proves nothing about the injection*; this adds *a test that reads the
wall clock at all is asserting against a "now" the code does not share.* One remedy covers both — inject
the clock, pin the date. ✔ Checked in production code and clean: the guard (`CommitteeSeatAuthority`) and
the report both use `Clock.system(UTC)`, so they share the **zone** as well as the predicate and the F2-62
divergence has not reopened through the clock. ⚙ Mutation could not have caught it — the harness ran six
named classes and this was not one of them: **a harness scoped to a slice's own tests cannot notice one of
those tests being wrong about the world.**

✔ **F2-175 CLOSED 2026-08-10 — `intake.intake_records` had two writers, and the second one's JSON was
invalid.** A CRITICAL model-drift observation opened a `RISK_ISSUE` intake by building the entity in
`MlModelDriftService` and calling `intakeRepo.save()`, so it consulted **none** of what F2-172 installed:
it hard-coded the assignee (`RISK_MANAGER`, a *role name* lifted from its own controller's `hasAnyRole`
guard, where the catalogue routes to `RISK_OFFICER`), minted its own `ISS-…` reference codes, did its own
`plusDays(14)` SLA arithmetic, wrote **no history events at all**, and hand-concatenated its payload with
a private `esc()`.

⚠⚠ **That last one was not cosmetic.** `esc()` escaped backslash, quote, `\n` and `\r`; JSON requires
**every** C0 control character escaped, and `IntakeService#contextFor` parses the payload before promotion.
So a CRITICAL drift on a model whose title carried a **tab** — the character a title acquires by being
pasted out of a spreadsheet — filed an issue that could **never be escalated into the risk register**,
reported as *"has an unreadable payload"* from `intake` while the fault sat in `ai/governance`. Verified
against Jackson before writing the fix, then live: a real tab in a real title, promoted end to end, with a
**negative control** proving the old payload is still refused.

⚠ **The filing said the bypass was "currently benign". The supportable claim was "unexercised".** Dev holds
26 drift observations, 2 CRITICAL, `triggered_issue_id` NULL on all 26, `IDENT_CURRENT` 27 over 26 rows —
seeded, never executed; `intake.intake_records` was at 0. 🔑 **A path that has never run cannot be observed
to be harmless, only to be untested** — and one of its five divergences was a break waiting for the first
real input.

⚠⚠ **The existing test asserted the defect as correct** — `startsWith("ISS-")`, `isEqualTo("SUBMITTED")`,
and a payload assertion (`contains("MODEL-2026-001")`) that a hand-built string satisfies whether or not it
parses. Second instance after [[F2-159]]. 🔑 **A test written by reading the implementation can only agree
with it**; the question it must answer is *should* the code do this, not *does* it.

⚙ **The fix is one construction site, not one call site.** The filing prescribed exposing
`submitSystemIntake(…)` and repointing the caller — necessary, not sufficient, because a second
`new IntakeRecord()` inside `IntakeService` is the same defect one file further in. `fileDraft(Draft)` is
now the only place in the platform an `IntakeRecord` is born, and the seam is an interface —
`intake.spi.SystemIntakePort`, the inbound counterpart to `RegisterPromotionPort`. `IntakeSingleWriterInvariantTest`
pins **one** construction site across 1,869 main sources, **one** repository user, and **no peer importing
anything of `module/intake` but its `spi`** — invariants, not ratchets, because the population is one and a
count to raise would make a tolerated writer indistinguishable from a reviewed one.

⚠ **Two of the filing's three architectural claims were false, and reading the guard cost five minutes.**
It said the edge crosses ADR-012 and that `ModuleGraphRatchetTest` should see it. ADR-018 homes `intake` in
**Base** and `ai/governance` is a sold SKU, so `ai → intake` is **SKU → Base, the legal direction**; and
that test's `KERNEL_ISH` set is `{platform, integrations, dashboard}`, so the edge is neither a kernel
inversion nor half of a cycle. What was violated is **encapsulation**, which nothing in this tree measured.

⚠⚠ **And "fixing" the assignee made it resolve to nobody — said plainly rather than dressed up.**
`RISK_MANAGER` exists in `iam.roles` and `rmanager` holds it; the catalogued `RISK_OFFICER` does not exist.
It is still the right change, for a reason that has to be *given*: `assigned_to` is a stakeholder-code
column, **10 of the catalogue's 14 codes are not role names**, and **nothing in `module/intake` resolves the
column at all** — it renders as a label. Nobody was notified before and nobody is now. What changed is that
the value agrees with the one catalogue [[F2-174]] can fix in a single place, and `IntakeCatalogueParityTest`
pins it field-by-field, so keeping `RISK_MANAGER` meant diverging from the pinned source of truth.

⚠⚠ **The live probe found a regression that 3,577 green tests and 17/17 mutations could not: a ROWVERSION
stale-update 500.** The old code did `save → open the issue → mutate → save AGAIN`, and it survived for as
long as it existed **only because nothing between the two saves forced a flush** — the issue was inserted
in the same persistence context, so Hibernate batched the observation's INSERT and UPDATE. Routing that
insert through the `@Transactional` port put a real boundary there, the flush happened, and the second
save's `UPDATE … WHERE row_version = <what this session last saw>` matched **zero rows**:
`StaleObjectStateException` → HTTP 500 on a governance escalation. Fixed by filing the issue **before** the
single `save()`; nothing in the payload ever needed the observation's id, so the second save was never
necessary. 🔑 **A latent double-save is not a style problem — it is a defect waiting for somebody to add a
transactional call between the two writes**, and CLAUDE.md's rule ("native first, mutate + save once") had
named only the loudest trigger for months. ⚠ **No unit test could see it: a mocked repository has no
`row_version`.** House rule 4 — *live-probe every slice* — paid for itself in one measurement, and the pin
is now `verify(driftRepo, times(1)).save(...)` plus an `InOrder` check.

⚙ **Writing a mutation exposed a test that could not fail:** `RISK_ISSUE`'s SLA is `24 * 14` hours, which
`plusDays(14)` equals exactly, so restoring the retired arithmetic survived. Fixed with a second case on
`WORKPLACE_INJURY` — the **24-hour** GOSI notification — where the two answers differ. The coincidence is
also why this never diverged visibly. ➕ Two unfiled defects fixed in passing: the payload **dropped
`notesAr`** (Arabic is mandatory, and it is the field carrying the analyst's own words), and the audit line
named the observation but **never the issue**, so a CRITICAL drift left no trace of the escalation.
`safeRole(String role) { return role; }` — a method named as if it validates, returning its argument —
deleted with the rest. 17 mutations, live probe **42/42**, 4 test classes, no migration, no frontend change.

⚠⚠ **And with the ROWVERSION fix in, the probe got one step further and found a SECOND defect: promoting a
`RISK_ISSUE` had never once worked.** `PUT …/triage` → **409**, and the backend log named it: *"The INSERT
statement conflicted with the CHECK constraint `CK_risks_status`… column 'status'"*. `RiskPromotionAdapter`
passed **`"IDENTIFIED"`**; the constraint allows `OPEN|UNDER_REVIEW|MITIGATING|ACCEPTED|CLOSED|ARCHIVED|
TRANSFERRED`. Its javadoc *argued* for `IDENTIFIED` — "raised, not assessed" — **right about the intent and
never a value the column accepts**. Fixed to `OPEN`; pinned by `RiskPromotionStatusTest`, which reads the
vocabulary out of the **migration SQL** so the unit suite stays database-free, and asserts the vocabulary is
non-empty first (its own first draft stripped every `N` from the literals and turned `OPEN` into `OPE` —
caught only by that anti-vacuity leg). ⚙ **Two independent reasons nobody had seen it:** F2-172 live-probed
promotion into `privacy.dpia` and reasoned about the other twelve adapters from their source; and the only
kind routed to `RISK` is `RISK_ISSUE`, whose sole producer was the drift monitor — the path this very slice
measured as never having run. 🔑 **A defect behind two blind spots is not found by probing either end.**
✅ Generalised and filed as **F2-180**, then **closed 2026-08-11** (see below): 1 of 13 adapters verified
working, 1 found broken, **11 unmeasured** — and a first attempt at a static sweep reported the broken one
as clean because it compared literals against *every* table's CHECKs rather than the target's.
⚠ **An unscoped cross-check is worse than none.**

---

### F2-180 — the other twelve adapters, measured instead of reasoned about ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-11

**13 of 13 adapters now verified live** (was 1 of 13), and the two that had never worked are fixed.

**What the scoped measurement found.** 13 adapters → 13 target tables → **18 single-column CHECK
vocabularies**, each literal compared against *its own* table's constraint:

- ⚠⚠ **`VendorPromotionAdapter` wrote `status = "ONBOARDING"`, which `CK_vendors_status` has never
  allowed** (`ACTIVE|INACTIVE|PENDING_REVIEW|TERMINATED`). Promoting a `VENDOR_ONBOARDING` submission had
  **never once worked**; all 28 vendors in dev are `ACTIVE`, which is what a register looks like when
  nothing has ever entered it through the front door. Fixed to `PENDING_REVIEW` — the vocabulary already
  had a word for "registered, reviews not yet done", so widening the CHECK would have taught every
  status-grouped query a new value to mean what an existing one already means.
- ⚠⚠ **`IncidentPromotionAdapter` passed the submitter's own category through untouched.** Measured against
  the forms its four kinds render: `SECURITY_INCIDENT` offers `PHISHING|MALWARE|LOST_DEVICE|
  UNAUTHORISED_ACCESS` — **0 of 4 legal**, so the flagship NCA ECC 6.1 employee-reporting path failed for
  every submission that answered the question. `WORKPLACE_INJURY`: 0 legal, fallback `"HSE"` not legal.
  `CONSUMER_COMPLAINT_RESPONSE`: **1 of 5** legal, fallback `"CONSUMER"` not legal. `VRP_DISCLOSURE` has no
  category field, fell through to `CYBER`, and was **the only one of the four that could ever promote.**
  Fixed by mapping the four vocabularies onto the column's five with per-kind fallbacks, and keeping the
  reporter's own word on the record — the **V261 precedent**, whose comment is the clearest statement of the
  rule in the tree: *"category → 'CYBER' (CK_incidents_category is strict; type kept in description)"*.

🔑 **Why it was three adapters and not eight.** Five constrained columns are fed by one accessor,
`IntakePromotionContext#severityOrMedium()`, which **clamps** to the four bands all five declare — written
by somebody who had checked. Category, status and change-type had no such accessor. So the lesson is not
"be careful with literals": **a closed column needs a closed writer, and the clamp is the only place that
can be.** `ck_change_type` was clamped here too although it was never failing — the form happens to offer
exactly the legal three, which is a fact about today's frontend, not a property of the server.

**⑤ The diagnostic that hid all of it.** **SQL Server error 547 is BOTH `FOREIGN KEY` and `CHECK`**, and
`GlobalExceptionHandler` answered with the foreign-key wording for both. Its own comment said
`// FOREIGN KEY / CHECK constraint`, so the ambiguity was known. Cost: F2-175 spent a probe iteration being
told a promotion failed on a **reference** in `risk.risks` — a table with **no foreign keys at all**;
F2-180 hit the same sentence on `CK_vendors_status`; then **19 more times** measuring F2-181. Now
`conflictKind: VALUE_NOT_ALLOWED` and *"One of the values supplied is not one this field accepts …
(column 'category')"*. The column is safe to name: the 547 CHECK message carries it **without** the
offending value, so SEC-CFG-001 still holds. 🔑 **A diagnostic that is wrong in a specific, plausible
direction is worse than a vague one: it does not slow the reader down, it sends them somewhere.**

**What shipped as the durable artefact.** `PromotionVocabularyTest` — hermetic (reads the migrations, so
`mvn -o clean package` stays database-free), keyed per **constraint** with a leg that proves from the
migration text that the constraint really is on that adapter's target table. Each constrained column is
**either** bound to the constant holding the value **or** listed in `unwritten` with a reason, which turns
the six targets whose tables carry no CHECK today into a pin rather than an omission: add one to
`privacy.dpia` and the build fails until somebody has looked at `DpiaPromotionAdapter`.

**⚠⚠ The unscoped-cross-check mistake recurred twice inside the slice that exists to fix it.** A heuristic
pairing UI option-lists to columns by value overlap produced 30+ "findings" including `VALID_NDI_TABS`
against `ck_change_risk` (both contain `CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW`) — discarded, with only the two
same-register pairings surviving into F2-181, each proven by a live POST. And the pin's own parser
extracted a column named **`PEND`** from `ratification_state <> N'PENDING'`, because `PENDING` contains
`IN`. Its `noUndeclaredConstrainedColumn` leg failed on the **first run** and named the phantom.
🔑 **A regex over SQL that has not had its string literals removed is parsing two languages at once.**

**Verification.** Suite **3,602/0/0** · mutation **15/15** (including binding an adapter to *another*
table's constraint whose vocabulary does contain the value, so only the scoping leg can catch it) · live
probe **50/50**, all 13 adapters submitting → promoting → reading the created row back by the id the server
stamped. The one leg that read as a failure was **the probe's own**: `ENGAGEMENT` returns the `external_id`,
not a bigint, exactly as `RegisterPromotionPort`'s javadoc allows. Corrected rather than explained away —
*a false negative in a verification artefact is worse than no leg, because it gets quoted.*

⬜ **F2-181 filed.** Asking who *else* writes the column F2-180's adapter was breaking found the register's
own create screen doing worse: `IncidentsPage.tsx` offers **22** categories and the column accepts **3**
(19 refused, live), plus **3 of 6** statuses — `CONTAINED`, `ERADICATED`, `RECOVERED`, the middle of the
NIST 800-61 lifecycle the screen is modelled on. Not bundled: the adapter's values were chosen by a
developer, so mapping them has one right answer; these are *offered to a user by the product*, and the fix
is either a migration widening a regulated register's taxonomy or the deletion of a deliberately-designed
one. ⚙ **A finding scoped to one producer should ask what the other producers of the same column do — the
scoping that makes an investigation tractable is also what hides its neighbour.**

⬜ **F2-179 filed, measured, and deliberately not bundled.** Repointing a caller means reading what it
*says*, and `severity` was the one field passed straight through — so: the escalation trigger is
`"CRITICAL".equals(req.severity())`, a case-**sensitive** Java comparison, while the column's CHECK
(`CK_ml_drift_sev`) runs under collation `Latin1_General_100_CI_AS_SC_UTF8`, which is case-**insensitive**.
Reproduced live: `severity: "critical"` → **201**, stored verbatim in lower case, `triggered_issue_id`
NULL, no intake row, and the model **still `IN_PRODUCTION`**. The controller's own javadoc says these
observations come from "automated monitoring jobs", which is precisely where casing conventions differ and
nobody reads the payload — and the failure is *silent*, so the first symptom is a critically drifted model
left in production. The [[F2-94]] class in a third disguise: **two artefacts that must agree, where one of
them cannot enforce the agreement.** Not bundled because the honest fix (normalise on write, so the CHECK,
the trigger and the frontend's label map all agree) sits next to a governance question — *should `MAJOR`
escalate too?* — and answering that while fixing a casing bug would smuggle a policy change in under a typo.

### F2-179 — the casing the constraint could not see, and the public portal it was hiding on ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-11

**The finding's own "look here next" pointer was wrong, and checking it is what found the real defect.**
The register row said to look at `ExerciseObserverService`, which holds the same five-token set against the
same collation. It is **already closed** — `normaliseRole`/`normaliseType`/`normaliseSeverity` each
`trim().toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT)` *before* testing the set, on every write path. It is the pattern to copy.
Third instance in this programme of a filing asserting something about existing code without opening it,
after F2-175's two false architectural claims and F2-178's recommendation for a report that had already
shipped. ⚙ **Read the code before believing a register row's claim about it — including one you wrote.**

**So the population was measured instead of guessed, and scoped deliberately.** 347 closed upper-case CHECK
vocabularies (of 389 single-column CHECKs), every text column case-insensitive → 207 reachable through an
entity field → **79 with an open writer** (a caller's casing reaches the column) → **25** also read back by
a case-sensitive Java comparison. **0** non-canonical values are stored in dev, so this is a latent trap
rather than damaged data — reachable only through the API, which is exactly where machine-to-machine callers
live. The join is `module(entity) == module(file) AND accessor-name == column-name`, narrow on purpose after
F2-180's unscoped-cross-check lesson; its one known imprecision produced exactly one false pairing
(`bcm.exercise_observation.severity`) and that is reported as such, not as a finding. ⚠ The scan reported
**0 of 389** on its first run, because `\b(IN|=)\b` can never match `=` — `=` is not a word character. The
anti-vacuity print is the only reason that surfaced as a bug instead of as "there is no population."

**⚠⚠ The severe instance was found by the sweep, not by the finding — and it is on the public portal.**
`WhistleblowerCaseService.submitCase` is unauthenticated, the widest caller surface in the product.
`isAnonymousReporterType` asked `"ANONYMOUS".equals(<the RAW request value>)`, so a reporter declaring
anonymity as `reporterType: "anonymous"` with the `isAnonymous` flag absent was recorded
`is_anonymous = FALSE` — and the next branch **persisted their name, email, phone and employee id.** Keeping
the reporter's identity out of the record is the one thing that module exists to do. Its sibling
`safeSeverity` switched case-sensitively and returned **`MEDIUM`** for `'critical'`, silently downgrading a
fraud or corruption allegation's triage band. And `safeChannel`/`safeReporterType` returned their argument
unchanged — the `safeRole(String role) { return role; }` decoy F2-175 deleted, **second instance, different
module. The name is the tell, not the module: grepping `safe*` immediately found a third** (`ComplaintService`,
filed as F2-183).

**Why the green suite missed the identity bug.** `submit_anonymousRequest_persistsTokenAndStripsContactFields`
asserts exactly the right thing and passes — because its fixture sets **both** `reporterType = "ANONYMOUS"`
*and* `isAnonymous = true`. The belt and the braces; the defect was in the braces alone. 🔑 **A fixture that
satisfies a condition twice cannot tell you which half is load-bearing.**

**What shipped.** `common/validation/ClosedVocabulary` — `require`/`orDefault`/`coerce`/`is`, refusing at
construction a set with no constraint name, lower-case tokens or no tokens, and at use a fallback outside its
own vocabulary. ⚙ **Not new code so much as code in the wrong package**: `CyberInputValidation#checkEnum` has
done this since CY-H, used 6 times, all inside `module/cyber`, which ADR-012/018 forbid a peer importing —
which is the whole reason every other module hand-rolled something weaker or nothing. The one addition that
matters: a vocabulary **names the CHECK it mirrors**, so `ClosedVocabularyPinTest` checks every one against
the migration SQL **by reflection** (never a source regex — F2-170's regex half matched a javadoc sentence
and reported 1,763 phantom failures), with no registry to forget to update.

**⚠ `require` vs `coerce` is a per-field product decision, not a house style.** Drift severity uses
`require`: a 400 beats a silently-defaulted governance signal. Whistleblower severity uses **`coerce`**,
because an unrecognised token was already accepted as `MEDIUM` and *the report arrived* — converting that to
a 400 would make submissions that succeed today start failing, which is the line `CyberInputValidation`'s own
javadoc draws. A lost whistleblower report is worse than a mis-graded one; for a governance escalation the
opposite holds. **The `MAJOR` question stays the owner's**, localised to one named constant.

**⚙ The migration parser was extracted, and the mutation harness earned its keep there.** Three test classes
had each grown a copy of the walk, so it became `support/MigrationVocabularies` (F2-178's predicate-sharing
lesson). The harness then found that **two of its safety rules mask each other**: drop the literal-stripping
and `ratification_state <> N'PENDING'` yields the phantom column `PEND`, but that makes the column count
*two*, so the multi-column rule discards the whole constraint instead of admitting the phantom — and every
downstream assertion stayed green. 🔑 **Two guards that each hide the other's failure are, between them, one
guard that nothing tests.** ⚠⚠ And it **corrected F2-180's own record**: that row credits the literal-stripping
with killing the `PEND` phantom, but the load-bearing half is the **word boundary** — `N'PENDING'` cannot
yield `PEND` while `\bIN\b` is required. Both parser mutations survive because the code is over-defended, not
under-tested; reported as **21/23 with both survivors explained** rather than 23/23 with a contrived test.
🔑 **When two changes ship together, only a mutation tells you which one was doing the work.**

**Verification.** Suite **3,633/0/0** · FE **487/487** in 50 files + `tsc` clean · mutation **21/23** ·
**live probe 31/31** on a jar-run backend (prod :8090 untouched): a `severity: "critical"` drift → 201 with
`triggeredIssueId` set (**NULL before**), the column byte-exact under `Latin1_General_100_BIN2` rather than
merely CI-equal, and the model flipped `IN_PRODUCTION → REVISION`; out-of-vocabulary values now **400 naming
the field and the offending value** where the CHECK answered 409; and 18 legs against the public portal with
**no `Authorization` header**, including the negative control that an identified reporter is still identified.
Cleanup by captured id plus a `CHARINDEX` belt, with an anti-vacuity leg that **failed on the first run**
because no whistleblower rows had been created — which is what makes "back to baseline" mean anything.
⚙ Two probe bugs cost one run each, and the platform's own diagnostics named both: `@Valid` firing before
`@PreAuthorize` on two required owner ids, and F2-83's 404 *"must carry a valid 'org' short code"* — the
counter-example to F2-180's foreign-key message. **0 migrations, 0 frontend change.**

✔ **F2-182 CLOSED 2026-08-11 — and the first act of working it was refuting its own headline.** The row,
written the previous day, listed **10** open writers and named two as control bypasses. Measured by reading
the code: **6 of the 10 were already closed, and neither bypass was reachable.** The scan behind the filing
called a writer *open* whenever the setter's argument came from the request, and a guard can sit in at least
four places it cannot see — a conjunction in the **same `if`** (`ndi`), a **shared `validate()`** called by
every mutation path (`kri`, `cma`, `tcfd`), an **`if` block** wrapping the setter (`bcm`), or a **DTO
annotation** (`sgi` create). 🔑 **"Is this writer closed?" is a dataflow question and a regex over setter
call sites cannot answer it** — it can only say where to go and read.

⚠ **The worst real site was the one the row described as "a dashboard KPI undercounts."**
`cyber.attack_surface_finding.severity`: `SEVERITY_WEIGHT.getOrDefault(severity, …get("LOW"))` scored an
asset carrying a lower-case `critical` finding at **15 instead of 100**, `pickHighestOpenSeverity` skipped
the row, and the critical-findings KPI omitted it — so an internet-facing asset with an open critical finding
read as the platform's **lowest** risk band. Probed live on one asset: **15.00 → 100.00**. That is the
inverted-indicator harm the row attributed to the KRI column, and unlike the KRI one it fails **open**.

⚙ **Two consequences the row overstated, corrected rather than quietly dropped.** `sgi_commitment.value_source`
could not actually trigger the refresh it "guards": `computeSourcedValue` switches on the same string, also
case-sensitively, so **a second case-sensitive comparison had accidentally neutralised the first one's
defect** — luck, not design. And `calendar_events.recurrence` did not pick the *wrong* RRULE; `rruleFor`'s
`default -> null` meant the `.ics` carried **no RRULE at all**, so a quarterly DR test subscribed once and
never again.

🔑 **The reusable rule this slice produced, which retires F2-179's per-field agonising for the whole family:**
ask whether a coercion **already exists upstream**. Where one does (the whistleblower portal's `safeSeverity`
returned `MEDIUM` and *the report arrived*), out-of-vocabulary values succeed today and `coerce` is mandatory.
Where none does, **the CHECK constraint is already refusing** everything outside the vocabulary — so every
value that succeeds today is a case-variant of a legal token and `require` **cannot break a working request**.
All five open sites were the second kind.

The two refuted sites (`ndi`, `kri`) were **closed anyway**, because both gate a control and both *read* the
column case-sensitively: a row arriving from a data fix, a restore or a future importer would have walked
through an NCA/NDI approval gate or inverted a KRI's bands. **Reachability is a fact about today, not a
property of a control.** Eight new `ClosedVocabulary` declarations, all agreeing with their migration CHECK on
the first run; `SgiCreateRequest`'s `@Pattern` and `CalendarEventDto`'s misplaced one both **deleted** so each
column has one authority. Durable half: **`HandRolledVocabularyMirrorTest`**, which reads the six hand-rolled
`Set` mirrors this slice deliberately left alone and compares them against their constraints — directional
(wider than the column fails, narrower is policy and is printed). Suite **3,671/0/0**, mutation **26/27** (the
survivor genuinely unkillable), live probe **43/43**, **0 migrations, 0 frontend change**.

⚠ **Two ways the mutation harness itself lied, both fixed.** It keyed backups per *edit*, so a mutation that
edits one file twice wrote its backup from the already-mutated text and **left the first edit in the tree** —
caught by `git status`, not by the harness. And a wrong assertion of mine left the baseline red, after which it
reported an SGI mutation as *"caught by a calendar test"*: **a mutation harness run against a red suite reports
every mutation as caught.** It now checks the baseline first and aborts if it is not green.

✔ **F2-184 CLOSED 2026-08-11 — filed as "plausibly P3" from one fail-closed instance; the measured population
was P2, and it indicted the slice that filed it.** Reflection over **2,941** types (254 controllers, 2,210
handlers — matching `LazyEntitySerialisationInvariantTest` exactly) found **405** types declaring a validation
constraint and **20 that nothing validates**. Against the **75** the abandoned regex claimed. Two false-positive
classes were excluded *with the reason stated*: test fixtures reached through `classpath*:`, and **JPA entities**,
whose constraints Hibernate's `BeanValidationEventListener` really does enforce at flush (a 500 rather than a
400, so worth knowing but not a bypass) — conflating those would have overstated the finding by six sites.

⚠⚠ **The worst instance was the only route that creates a sanctions entry.** `EntryBulkImportRequest.entries`
was `@NotNull` but not `@Valid`, and `EntryCreateRequest` is bound **only** there — no single-entry endpoint
exists. So `@NotBlank primaryNameEn`, `@NotBlank entryExternalId` and the `@Pattern`s on `entityType`/`severity`
never ran; the service is a setter copy guarded only by `assertWritable`; and `aml.sanctions_list_entry` has
**zero CHECKs**, so those patterns were the *only* narrowing. **A sanctions entry with a blank name is stored and
never matches a screening query.** It also closed a second defect for free: the duplicate check is
`existsBy…EntryExternalId(null)` → `= NULL` → never true, so null-id entries were **created, not skipped, on
every re-import**. Fixing the boundary made that query unreachable.

🔑 **The rule, and it is not "add `@Valid` everywhere":** a dormant `@Size` number has never been tested against
its column, so enabling it is a decision. Cap **==** column → enable (converts a truncation 500 into a named 400
and cannot break a working request). Column **NVARCHAR(MAX)** → the schema deliberately leaves it unbounded, so
**delete the cap** — `AttendanceMark.coiNote`'s was deleted for exactly this reason, because capping a
conflict-of-interest declaration is a product change. Cap **looser** than the column → the annotation is what is
wrong. Third variant of one question: F2-179 asked it per field, F2-182 answered it with *does a coercion exist
upstream*, F2-184 with *does anything already refuse this*. Every enabled constraint was checked against stored
data first (15 sanctions rows, 40 loss lines, 0 negatives), so this is latent-defect closure, not a behaviour
change.

⚠ **And it found four more inert constraints on `CalendarEventDto` — the class F2-182 had already fixed**,
sitting above the comment F2-182 wrote about deleting the fifth. 🔑 **Fixing the instance you noticed is not
closing the shape, and a class you have already edited reads as one you have already checked.** That is the whole
case for the instrument over the read.

Gate: `InertValidationConstraintTest` holds the 12 survivors as a **named map with a reason each, enforced in
both directions** — a new one fails the build, and a fixed one must have its entry removed. A decrease-only "12"
would let one be swapped for another, the failure CLAUDE.md records for `BARE_EXPORT_CEILING`. Six of the 16
mutations attack the instrument itself, including **the phantom-75 bug** (attributing a nested type's constraints
to its container), so the defect that made this a filing rather than a sweep cannot come back silently.
Suite **3,687/0/0**, mutation **16/16**, live probe **37/37** as `compliance`, 0 migrations, 0 FE change.

⬜ **F2-185 — retaliation half RESOLVED 2026-08-11, vendor-BCP half still OPEN.** ⚠⚠ **The P2 this row carried
was based on a false claim, and a live probe settled it 20/20.** It said *"a retaliation complaint cannot be closed
through the API"* — it can: `POST /retaliation/{id}/validate|uphold|dismiss` are all wired, guarded

VALIDATED → UPHELD` and `RECEIVED → DISMISSED` both complete against the running stack; an illegal jump still 409s;
`ranalyst` gets 403. So `transitionTo` was a redundant **fourth** path and was **deleted**, not wired — its DTO added
nothing (`terminalStatus` is what the path encodes, `assignedProtectorUserId` is the query param the three already
take) and its audit line read *"transitioned to UPHELD"* where `uphold()` writes *"upheld — disciplinary action
triggered"*, the sentence a labour regulator reads. 🔑 **A dark method is not automatically a missing capability;
sort by EFFECT, not by verb name** (F2-165's own correction). 🔑 **The wrong claim came from reading the service and
not the controller beside it** — one file short is the whole error, the same shape as F2-179's "`ExerciseObserverService`
is open", and both were mine. **Still open:** `VendorBcpAttestationDtos.EscalateRequest`, which unlike its sibling has

call. ⚠ Do **not** close it by deleting the inert `@Size`. ⚠ One correction carried forward:
`ApproveAccessRequest.overrideJustification` is `@Size(max = 1000)`, **not** `@NotBlank` — I was one step from
recording "an override can be approved with no justification" before reading the DTO. **The severity of an inert

🔑 **A green reachability gate certifies the granularity it resolves and nothing coarser or finer.**

`generateQuarterlyReport` picks the SAMA-facing `topCategory` with

but bucket order depends on the map's insertion history. ⚠ Not fixed with F2-183 because the tie-break is

asserting the implementation rather than the requirement** — F2-183's first draft did, and rebuilding the
fixture as 3-versus-2 is what surfaced this.

`lib/platformPersistence.ts` declared a three-mode switch (`'demo' | 'rest' | 'mixed'`) and exported
three `mirror*ToBackend` helpers that return immediately in `'demo'` mode. Measured:
**`setPersistenceMode` had ZERO callers in the product, nothing wrote `grc.persistence.mode.v1`, and
the switch took no Vite env input** — so `'demo'` was an *invariant*, not a default, and all three
helpers were unconditional no-ops called from **11 sites across 5 modules**. The READ path never
consulted the mode at all, so even a reachable switch could not have displayed what it wrote.
🔑 **Writing to a store you never read from is not persistence, it is a one-way drain.**

⚠⚠ **The topbar badge reads a DIFFERENT switch.** `lib/productionMode.ts` (key `grc.mode.v1`) does
take `VITE_MODE`, so a deployment could set `VITE_MODE=production`, turn the badge green and label it
"Production", while the switch gating every lifecycle write stayed `'demo'` and unreachable.
`platformPersistence.ts`'s own header claimed it drove that badge. It did not, and never had.
